title: Phenotypic plasticity supports green tide persistence before bioenergetic failure underlies terminal decline
content:
Abstract

Trans-regional green tides dominated by Ulva prolifera exert significant impacts on coastal ecosystems. While the mechanisms of early-stage proliferation are well documented, the specific physiological and molecular drivers governing the transition from bloom persistence to terminal decline during this trans-regional drift remain unresolved. Using in situ physiological and transcriptomic data collected across a 300-km latitudinal gradient in the Yellow Sea, we found that a dominant molecular type (5S-II) within the sampled 2021 U. prolifera population showed phenotypic plasticity, with its physiological and transcriptional traits varying across environmental conditions. Physiological observations showed declines in photosynthetic performance (F v /F m and rETR) and pigment content along the northward drift path, marking a transition from active growth to physiological decline. Transcriptomic and physiological evidence further indicated that the intermediate drifting phase was characterized by a compensatory photoprotective state, potentially involving cyclic electron flow. By contrast, terminal-phase stress was associated with reduced expression of G-protein-signaling-related genes and patterns suggesting that PSII repair could no longer compensate for photodamage as energy metabolism declined. This bioenergetic failure coincided with a shift toward endogenous catabolism and a transition from vegetative growth toward sporulation. Together, these findings provide insight into bloom termination and suggest that ocean warming may accelerate late-stage senescence, whereas acidification may intensify photosynthetic inhibition under multiple stressors, potentially increasing coastal hypoxia risk.
